extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph). Covers how examiners should analyze original, new, and amended claims for adequate support in the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description separate from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (and pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1) require that 'the specification shall contain a written description of the invention ....' This requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: (1) to clearly convey that the applicant invented the claimed subject matter; (2) to put the public in possession of what is claimed; and (3) to describe the technology adequately in exchange for the right to exclude others. Cite authorities: Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly; Vas-Cath v. Mahurkar; Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient detail to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas. A showing of possession alone does not cure lack of written description. Case examples: Moba v. Diamond Automation; Vas-Cath; Enzo Biochem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by describing all claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be demonstrated by actual reduction to practice, or by showing invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen v. Chugai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposits are corroborative but not substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference in the specification to a deposit may satisfy written description with respect to a claimed material, but such a deposit is not a substitute for the written description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written description of deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds on written disclosure. Deposits made after filing cannot be relied upon to support additions or corrections except under narrow regulatory conditions (37 CFR 1.801 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims presumed adequate but may lack particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; however, the claimed invention as a whole may not be adequately described if an essential or critical feature is not described with sufficient particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner initially bears burden to present reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as supporting the claims (In re Wertheim). Example: claim 'A gene comprising SEQ ID NO:1' may implicitly include promoters or regulatory elements that are not described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language insufficient for some biomolecules
rubrics_metrics.description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without any known or disclosed correlation between that function and the structure of the sequence, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing method of obtaining a claimed sequence without structural identification is typically insufficient. Compare software disclosure (functions may suffice where writing code is within skill of the art). See In re Bell, In re Deuel, Fonar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species and 'laundry list' limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'laundry list' disclosure of every possible moiety does not necessarily constitute a written description of every species in a genus because it would not 'reasonably lead' those skilled in the art to any particular species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If knowledge and level of skill would not permit one skilled in the art to immediately envisage the claimed product from the process or genus disclosure, written description may be inadequate. (Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; Purdue Pharma v. Faulding).

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations that are not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement (and may constitute improper new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support for new limitations may be express, implicit, or inherent. Applicant may amend specification to include claimed subject matter present in original claims. Correction of obvious typographical errors is allowed when one skilled in the art would recognize and correct the error. See In re Rasmussen; In re Benno; In re Oda; MPEP §§2163.06-07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections to sequencing errors and deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to sequencing errors, corrections may be permissible where the application included sequence information and references a deposit made in compliance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; deposits made after the application filing date generally cannot be relied upon to support additions or corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor sequence errors may be correctable if one skilled in the art would immediately recognize the minor error and resequence the deposited material. Post-filing deposits can support corrections only if applicant complies with 37 CFR 1.804 and related statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an essential limitation can invalidate broader claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits matter disclosed as essential or critical in the specification may fail the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims broadened by removing location of a control means where specification stated location was 'the only possible location' (Gentry Gallery); omitting an element applicant described as essential may also lead to enablement or indefiniteness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description is a question of fact (case-by-case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the written description requirement is essentially a fact-based inquiry that will 'necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve by case-by-case factual analysis considering the nature of the invention and the knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art by the disclosure. (Enzo Biochem; Vas-Cath; AbbVie Deutschland v. Janssen Biotech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden to make a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption of adequate written description, so the examiner has the initial burden, after thorough reading and evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize that the written description supports the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a prima facie case the examiner need not present factual evidence but must point out claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why. Hyatt v. Dudas: examiner listed each element of unsupported combination, shifting burden to applicant to show support or amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must identify support for amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant amends claims, applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; applicant should specifically point out where the originally filed disclosure supports the amendment(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant points out support and examiner still finds disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, examiner has the initial burden of explaining why persons skilled in the art would not recognize support. (MPEP §2163.04; Hyatt).

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is essential: each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description. The entire claim — preamble, transitional phrase, and body — must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction affects written description analysis. Consider transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and preamble weight. Cites: Katz; In re Morris; Genentech v. Chiron; MPEP §2111.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sufficiency of recited structures, acts, or functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should evaluate if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given to the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are described, lack of adequate description of their particular combination can support a prima facie lack of written description (Hyatt). Preamble may be structural limitation depending on application. See Bell Communications; Corning Glass Works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase treatment and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') affect claim scope; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate and may be construed as 'comprising' for prior art purposes absent clear specification limiting what would materially affect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant bears burden to show that inclusion of additional components would materially change characteristics. See Genentech; PPG Indus.; AK Steel; MPEP §2111.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims require disclosure of combination, not just parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a particular combination of elements requires that the written description adequately describe that particular combination, not merely the individual elements in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should point out if the claimed combination is not adequately described; applicant must then identify where the combination is supported or amend. (Hyatt; Stored Value Solutions example where three authorization codes were essential claim limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency as a basis for support
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, an application necessarily discloses that function, theory, or advantage, and the application may later be amended to recite it without new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. (In re Reynolds; In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference treated as part of application
rubrics_metrics.description: Information incorporated by reference into the specification is as much a part of the application as if the text were repeated in the application; replacing the incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP §608.01(p). Consider impact on 35 U.S.C. 112(b) / 112(f) analyses per MPEP §2181 and related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support for priority/benefit claims and interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate written description issues arise when determining whether a claimed invention is entitled to the benefit of an earlier priority or effective filing date, or whether the specification provides support for claims corresponding to an interference count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate original disclosure for support of subject matter for priority under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365, 386 and for interference counts; see cited case law (New Railhead; Tronzo; Fiers; In re Ziegler; Martin v. Mayer; Fields v. Conover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical examiner methodology — read, analyze, and point out deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should thoroughly read and evaluate the content of the application and, where appropriate, present reasons or evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize support for the claims; point out unsupported claim limitations and explain deficiencies to make a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner practices include: analyze each claim separately, construe claims broadly reasonable in light of specification, list unsupported limitations, reference relevant MPEP sections and case law, and consider enablement/other statutory requirements in tandem before completing office action that includes a written description rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claim (preamble, transitional language) must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim as a whole, including preamble language and transitional phrase, must be sufficiently supported to satisfy the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble language may be structural and part of invention depending on entire disclosure; examiner should determine how much weight preamble receives by reviewing whole application. See Pac-Tec; Corning Glass Works; MPEP §2111.
